'''Michelle C. Y. Chang''' (born 1977) is the A. Barton Hepburn Professor of Chemistry at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michelle Chang – Princeton University Department of Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty-research/faculty/michelle-chang/ |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=chemistry.princeton.edu}}</ref> She is the recipient of several young scientist awards for her research in [[biosynthesis]] of [[biofuel]]s and [[pharmaceutical]]s.''<ref name="ucb">{{cite web |title=Faculty & Research - College of Chemistry |url=http://chem.berkeley.edu/faculty/chang_m/index.php |website=chem.berkeley.edu}}</ref>'' Previously, she was a Professor of Chemistry and Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], before moving her lab to Princeton in January 2024.<ref name="chemistry.princeton.edu">{{Cite web |title=Michelle Chang Joins Princeton Chemistry – Princeton University Department of Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/news/michelle-chang-joins-princeton-chemistry-faculty/ |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=chemistry.princeton.edu}}</ref>

==Education==
Chang received her [[B.S.]] in biochemistry and [[B.A.]] in French literature from the [[University of California, San Diego]], in 1997.

She then moved to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] for graduate school as a [[National Science Foundation]] Predoctoral Fellow (1997-2000) and M.I.T./[[Merck & Co.|Merck]] Foundation Predoctoral Fellow (2000-2002). She earned her Ph.D. in 2004 under the direction of [[JoAnne Stubbe]] and [[Daniel G. Nocera]]. During her graduate work, Chang studied [[proton-coupled electron transfer]] processes in [[ribonucleotide reductase]] enzymes, and demonstrated the first direct evidence of the radical transfer pathway of class I RNRs.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Proton-coupled electron transfer in the Escherichia coli ribonucleotide reductase|url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/30067|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=2004|degree=|first=Michelle C. Y. (Michelle Chia-yu)|last=Chang|hdl=1721.1/30067}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Michelle C. Y.|last2=Yee|first2=Cyril S.|last3=Stubbe|first3=JoAnne|last4=Nocera|first4=Daniel G.|date=2004-05-04|title=Turning on ribonucleotide reductase by light-initiated amino acid radical generation|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=101|issue=18|pages=6882–6887|doi=10.1073/pnas.0401718101|issn=0027-8424|pmid=15123822|pmc=406436|bibcode=2004PNAS..101.6882C|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Michelle C. Y.|last2=Yee|first2=Cyril S.|last3=Nocera|first3=Daniel G.|last4=Stubbe|first4=JoAnne|date=2004-12-01|title=Site-Specific Replacement of a Conserved Tyrosine in Ribonucleotide Reductase with an Aniline Amino Acid: A Mechanistic Probe for a Redox-Active Tyrosine|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja044124d|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=126|issue=51|pages=16702–16703|doi=10.1021/ja044124d|pmid=15612690|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Following graduate school, she conducted research as a [[Jane Coffin Childs Memorial Fund for Medical Research]] Postdoctoral Fellow at [[University of California, Berkeley]] with [[Jay Keasling]] (2004-2007). At Berkeley, Chang studied enzyme-catalyzed reactions, demonstrating that by expressing plant [[Cytochrome P450|P450]] enzymes in bacteria like ''E. coli'', the ''[[Escherichia coli|E. coli]]'' could be engineered to produce [[terpenoid]]s, a class of natural products often found in drugs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Michelle Chang: A catalyst for change|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/scientist-to-watch-old/michelle-chang-a-catalyst-for-change-44415|access-date=2021-05-15|website=The Scientist Magazine®|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=Michelle C. Y.|last2=Eachus|first2=Rachel A.|last3=Trieu|first3=William|last4=Ro|first4=Dae-Kyun|last5=Keasling|first5=Jay D.|date=2007|title=Engineering Escherichia coli for production of functionalized terpenoids using plant P450s|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nchembio875|journal=Nature Chemical Biology|language=en|volume=3|issue=5|pages=274–277|doi=10.1038/nchembio875|pmid=17438551|issn=1552-4469|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Chang began her independent career at UC Berkeley in 2007. She joined the faculty at Princeton University in 2024.<ref name="chemistry.princeton.edu"/>

==Personal life==
Michelle was born in [[San Diego, California|San Diego]], [[California]], to Chinese immigrant parents from [[Taiwan]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.pchome.com.tw/finance/cnyes/20110311/index-12998026413899109003.html|title=財經新聞 - PChome 新聞|website=PChome 新聞}}</ref> She is married to her colleague in the [[UC Berkeley College of Chemistry|College of Chemistry]], [[Christopher Chang]].<ref>[http://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/article/18442 "National magazines tout two chemists and two astronomers as top innovators in their fields"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613182410/http://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/article/18442 |date=2011-06-13 }}, UC Newsroom, August 22, 2008 (retrieved January 26, 2010)</ref>
